claim: Baseline AMPAR expression in individual spines is highly dynamic in primary visual cortex (V1) layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons.
source: We observed that baseline AMPAR expression in individual spines is highly dynamic with more dynamics in primary visual cortex (V1) layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons than V1 L5 neurons.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing dynamic changes in spine sGluA1 expression over time in V1 L2/3 neurons.

claim: Baseline AMPAR expression in individual spines shows more dynamics in V1 L2/3 neurons than V1 L5 neurons.
source: We observed that baseline AMPAR expression in individual spines is highly dynamic with more dynamics in primary visual cortex (V1) layer 2/3 (L2/3) neurons than V1 L5 neurons.
evidence: Supported by comparison of CV of spine sGluA1 signal between L2/3 and L5 neurons showing L2/3 has higher dynamics.

claim: Visual deprivation through binocular enucleation induces a synapse-specific change of synaptic AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons.
source: Visual deprivation through binocular enucleation induces a synapse-specific and depth-dependent change of synaptic AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons, wherein deep synapses are potentiated more than superficial synapses.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing heterogeneous responses of individual spines to visual deprivation.

claim: Visual deprivation through binocular enucleation induces a depth-dependent change of synaptic AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons.
source: Visual deprivation through binocular enucleation induces a synapse-specific and depth-dependent change of synaptic AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons, wherein deep synapses are potentiated more than superficial synapses.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing positive correlation between spine depth and deprivation-induced sGluA1 expression changes.

claim: Deep synapses are potentiated more than superficial synapses following visual deprivation in V1 L2/3 neurons.
source: Visual deprivation through binocular enucleation induces a synapse-specific and depth-dependent change of synaptic AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons, wherein deep synapses are potentiated more than superficial synapses.
evidence: Supported by data showing that spines positioned more deeply exhibited greater deprivation-induced changes in synaptic sGluA1 expression.

claim: The increase in synaptic AMPARs following visual deprivation is specific to L2/3 neurons and absent on apical dendrites of L5 neurons.
source: The increase is specific to L2/3 neurons and absent on apical dendrites of L5 neurons, and is dependent on expression of the AMPAR-binding protein GRIP1.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing significant increases in spine sGluA1 in L2/3 neurons but not in L5 neurons following visual deprivation.

claim: The increase in synaptic AMPARs following visual deprivation is dependent on expression of the AMPAR-binding protein GRIP1.
source: The increase is specific to L2/3 neurons and absent on apical dendrites of L5 neurons, and is dependent on expression of the AMPAR-binding protein GRIP1.
evidence: Supported by data showing no increase in synaptic GluA1 in Grip1 knockout mice following visual deprivation.

claim: Specific neuronal connections across cortical layers respond uniquely to changes in sensory experience.
source: Our study demonstrates that specific neuronal connections, across cortical layers and even within individual neurons, respond uniquely to changes in sensory experience.
evidence: Supported by data showing differential responses between L2/3 and L5 neurons and between apical and basal dendrites.

claim: Specific neuronal connections within individual neurons respond uniquely to changes in sensory experience.
source: Our study demonstrates that specific neuronal connections, across cortical layers and even within individual neurons, respond uniquely to changes in sensory experience.
evidence: Supported by data showing different responses between apical and basal dendrites of the same L2/3 neurons.

claim: Chronic visual deprivation through monocular eyelid suture induces an initial decline in activity of pyramidal neurons in the visual cortex that is eventually restored to baseline.
source: The homeostatic regulation of neuronal activity has been demonstrated in vivo, where chronic visual deprivation through monocular eyelid suture induces an initial decline in activity of pyramidal neurons in the visual cortex that is eventually restored to baseline (Hengen et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Hengen et al.

claim: Recovery of neuronal activity following enucleation is accompanied by an increase in spine size.
source: Other studies using enucleation to deprive the vision show that the recovery of neuronal activity is accompanied by an increase in spine size (Barnes et al., 2015; Keck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Barnes et al. and Keck et al.

claim: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are the principle postsynaptic glutamate receptors mediating fast excitatory synaptic transmission.
source: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are the principle postsynaptic glutamate receptors mediating fast excitatory synaptic transmission, and regulation of AMPAR trafficking is critical for synaptic plasticity and brain function (Diering and Huganir, 2018; Volk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to review articles.

claim: Regulation of AMPAR trafficking is critical for synaptic plasticity and brain function.
source: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are the principle postsynaptic glutamate receptors mediating fast excitatory synaptic transmission, and regulation of AMPAR trafficking is critical for synaptic plasticity and brain function (Diering and Huganir, 2018; Volk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to review articles.

claim: Chronic visual deprivation induces up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs in the primary visual cortex in vitro and ex vivo.
source: One of the major forms of homeostatic regulation of neuronal activity involves the modulation of AMPAR expression at synapses and this has been extensively characterized in vitro and ex vivo (Desai et al., 2002; Goel et al., 2006; Goel and Lee, 2007; O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano, 2012; Turrigiano et al., 1998), where chronic visual deprivation induces up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs in the primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: There is a high correlation between spine intensity of SEP-GluA1 and glutamate uncaging-evoked excitatory postsynaptic current (uEPSC) amplitude.
source: First, we found a high correlation between spine intensity of SEP-GluA1 and glutamate uncaging-evoked excitatory postsynaptic current (uEPSC) amplitude (Figure 1C,D), suggesting that spine enrichment of SEP-GluA1 largely reflects postsynaptic strength.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glutamate uncaging experiments shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Spine enrichment of SEP-GluA1 largely reflects postsynaptic strength.
source: First, we found a high correlation between spine intensity of SEP-GluA1 and glutamate uncaging-evoked excitatory postsynaptic current (uEPSC) amplitude (Figure 1C,D), suggesting that spine enrichment of SEP-GluA1 largely reflects postsynaptic strength.
evidence: Inferred from the high correlation between SEP-GluA1 intensity and uEPSC amplitude.

claim: The majority of spines in V1 L2/3 neurons (68%) persisted throughout all 10 imaging days.
source: We found that the majority of spines in V1 L2/3 neurons (68%) persisted throughout all 10 imaging days (Figure 1F), comparable to previous reports (Holtmaat et al., 2005), suggesting that the modest overexpression of AMPARs does not affect spine dynamics.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The modest overexpression of AMPARs does not affect spine dynamics.
source: We found that the majority of spines in V1 L2/3 neurons (68%) persisted throughout all 10 imaging days (Figure 1F), comparable to previous reports (Holtmaat et al., 2005), suggesting that the modest overexpression of AMPARs does not affect spine dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that spine survival rate is comparable to previous reports without AMPAR overexpression.

claim: Total spine surface GluA1 (sGluA1) levels on a dendrite were stable over 10 days in adult animals.
source: Total spine surface GluA1 (sGluA1) levels on a dendrite, average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size in persistent spines were all stable (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Average spine sGluA1 expression in persistent spines was stable over 10 days in adult animals.
source: Total spine surface GluA1 (sGluA1) levels on a dendrite, average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size in persistent spines were all stable (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Spine size in persistent spines was stable over 10 days in adult animals.
source: Total spine surface GluA1 (sGluA1) levels on a dendrite, average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size in persistent spines were all stable (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In adult animals, overall expression of spine sGluA1 expression remains constant throughout daily imaging sessions.
source: These results show that in adult animals, overall expression of spine sGluA1 expression remains constant throughout daily imaging sessions.
evidence: Supported by data showing stable total and average spine sGluA1 levels over 10 days.

claim: sGluA1 intensity within individual persistent spines was highly dynamic and varied over days.
source: We observed that sGluA1 intensity within individual persistent spines was highly dynamic and varied over days (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by heat map data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The relative sGluA1 level in individual spines at day 1 remained strongly correlated with their level at day 10.
source: Despite the dynamic expression across days, the relative sGluA1 level in individual spines at day 1 remained strongly correlated with their level at day 10 (Figure 2B), indicating that the difference in sGluA1 level between persistent spines doesn't change over time with strong spines remaining strong and weak spines staying weak.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in sGluA1 level between persistent spines doesn't change over time with strong spines remaining strong and weak spines staying weak.
source: Despite the dynamic expression across days, the relative sGluA1 level in individual spines at day 1 remained strongly correlated with their level at day 10 (Figure 2B), indicating that the difference in sGluA1 level between persistent spines doesn't change over time with strong spines remaining strong and weak spines staying weak.
evidence: Inferred from the strong correlation between day 1 and day 10 sGluA1 levels.

claim: There were no correlations between CV of spine sGluA1 signal and initial spine sGluA1 level.
source: Intriguingly, we did not observe any correlations between CV of spine sGluA1 signal and their initial spine sGluA1 level (Figure 2C), suggesting that all spines show similar extent of dynamics despite their variances in sGluA1 levels.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All spines show similar extent of dynamics despite their variances in sGluA1 levels.
source: Intriguingly, we did not observe any correlations between CV of spine sGluA1 signal and their initial spine sGluA1 level (Figure 2C), suggesting that all spines show similar extent of dynamics despite their variances in sGluA1 levels.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of correlation between CV and initial sGluA1 level.

claim: The CV of V1 L2/3 neurons became significantly smaller after visual deprivation.
source: We found that the CV of V1 L2/3 neurons became significantly smaller after deprivation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data comparing CV before and after visual deprivation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AMPAR dynamics in individual spines is partially driven by sensory input.
source: This demonstrates that AMPAR dynamics in individual spines is partially driven by sensory input.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CV decreased after visual deprivation.

claim: Both newly formed and eliminated spines had significantly lower sGluA1 expression compared with persistent spines on the same dendrite.
source: We also characterized sGluA1 expression in non-persistent (transient) spines that were newly formed or eliminated, and observed that both groups of spines had significantly lower sGluA1 expression compared with persistent spines on the same dendrite (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E,F comparing sGluA1 levels in transient and persistent spines.

claim: Newly formed spines gradually increased sGluA1 levels after formation.
source: Nevertheless, newly formed spines gradually increased sGluA1 levels after formation, while eliminated spines significantly decreased sGluA1 content prior to elimination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Eliminated spines significantly decreased sGluA1 content prior to elimination.
source: Nevertheless, newly formed spines gradually increased sGluA1 levels after formation, while eliminated spines significantly decreased sGluA1 content prior to elimination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CV of spine sGluA1 expression in transient spines was much higher than that in persistent spines.
source: The CV of spine sGluA1 expression in transient spines was much higher than that in persistent spines (Figure 2G), suggesting that GluA1 levels on transient spines are more dynamic than on persistent spines.
evidence: Supported by data comparing CV between transient and persistent spines shown in Figure 2G.

claim: GluA1 levels on transient spines are more dynamic than on persistent spines.
source: The CV of spine sGluA1 expression in transient spines was much higher than that in persistent spines (Figure 2G), suggesting that GluA1 levels on transient spines are more dynamic than on persistent spines.
evidence: Inferred from the higher CV in transient spines.

claim: sGluA1 level largely reflects spine stability.
source: These results indicate that sGluA1 level largely reflects spine stability.
evidence: Inferred from observations that transient spines have lower sGluA1 and higher CV than persistent spines.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between spine size and spine sGluA1 intensity in vivo.
source: Consistent with previous in vitro studies, we found a strong positive correlation between spine size and spine sGluA1 intensity in vivo (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There is a highly positive correlation between the daily change of spine size and sGluA1 change.
source: Moreover, there was a highly positive correlation between the daily change of spine size and sGluA1 change (Figure 2I), indicating that spine size and GluA1 expression increase or decrease concurrently.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Spine size and GluA1 expression increase or decrease concurrently.
source: Moreover, there was a highly positive correlation between the daily change of spine size and sGluA1 change (Figure 2I), indicating that spine size and GluA1 expression increase or decrease concurrently.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between daily changes in spine size and sGluA1.

claim: A small fraction of spines (~18%) show an inverse correlation between daily spine size change and sGluA1 change.
source: However, we identified a small fraction of spines (~18%) that show an inverse correlation between daily spine size change and sGluA1 change (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Spines with inverse correlation between daily spine size change and sGluA1 change tend to be spines with lower sGluA1 level.
source: We further examined the sGluA1 level distribution of those spines and found that there was a significant leftward shift of sGluA1 level distribution in those subsets of spines compared to all spines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that they tend to be spines with lower sGluA1 level.
evidence: Supported by distribution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Enucleation did not affect dendritic dsRed2 signal.
source: Enucleation did not affect dendritic dsRed2 signal nor spine survival rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Enucleation did not affect spine survival rate.
source: Enucleation did not affect dendritic dsRed2 signal nor spine survival rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons decreased 1 day after enucleation.
source: However, the average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons decreased 1 day after enucleation, recovered at day 2, and significantly increased by day 7 (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons recovered at day 2 after enucleation.
source: However, the average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons decreased 1 day after enucleation, recovered at day 2, and significantly increased by day 7 (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons significantly increased by day 7 after enucleation.
source: However, the average synaptic sGluA1 level in persistent spines of V1 neurons decreased 1 day after enucleation, recovered at day 2, and significantly increased by day 7 (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The changes of spine size following visual deprivation showed similar trends to sGluA1 but with smaller changes.
source: The changes of spine size showed similar trends but with smaller changes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C comparing spine size changes to sGluA1 changes.

claim: There were no significant increases of sGluA1 expression in non-V1 visual cortex following 7 days of enucleation.
source: We also imaged spines in visual cortical regions outside of V1 (non-V1) and found that there were no significant increases of sGluA1 expression, as well as spine size, in non-V1 visual cortex following 7 days of enucleation (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: There were no significant increases of spine size in non-V1 visual cortex following 7 days of enucleation.
source: We also imaged spines in visual cortical regions outside of V1 (non-V1) and found that there were no significant increases of sGluA1 expression, as well as spine size, in non-V1 visual cortex following 7 days of enucleation (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A systematic decrease in sGluA1 level was observed after visual deprivation in non-V1 visual cortex regions.
source: Indeed, we observed a systematic decrease in sGluA1 level after VD in those regions (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Visual deprivation-induced spine enrichment of sGluA1 is specific to V1.
source: These data demonstrate that visual deprivation-induced spine enrichment of sGluA1 is specific to V1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sGluA1 increased in V1 but not in non-V1 visual cortex after deprivation.

claim: The responses of individual dendrites to visual deprivation were highly heterogeneous.
source: We found that the responses of individual dendrites and spines were highly heterogeneous (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by heat map data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses of individual spines to visual deprivation were highly heterogeneous.
source: We found that the responses of individual dendrites and spines were highly heterogeneous (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by heat map data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only a subset of spines undergo potentiation following visual deprivation.
source: Despite the overall increase in spine sGluA1 expression after 7 days of deprivation, some dendrites or spines did reduce sGluA1 expression (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), indicating that only a subset of spines undergo potentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the heterogeneous responses showing some spines increase while others decrease.

claim: A greater proportion of dendrites underwent increases in sGluA1 following visual deprivation compared to control mice with sham-surgery.
source: However, compared to control mice with sham-surgery (SH), a greater proportion of dendrites or spines underwent increases (Figure 4A, B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by histogram data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a very strong positive correlation between spine sGluA1 changes of individual dendrites at day 1 and at day 7 after enucleation.
source: Therefore, we examined the relationship between spine sGluA1 changes of individual dendrites at day 1 and at day 7 after enucleation. A very strong positive correlation was detected (Figure 4C), indicating that dendrites that display a rapid decrease at day 1 would remain decreased at day 7 or show a reduced increase by day 7.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dendrites that display a rapid decrease at day 1 would remain decreased at day 7 or show a reduced increase by day 7.
source: Therefore, we examined the relationship between spine sGluA1 changes of individual dendrites at day 1 and at day 7 after enucleation. A very strong positive correlation was detected (Figure 4C), indicating that dendrites that display a rapid decrease at day 1 would remain decreased at day 7 or show a reduced increase by day 7.
evidence: Inferred from the strong positive correlation between day 1 and day 7 changes.

claim: There are two populations of dendrites with distinct responses to visual deprivation: one population showed decrease of sGluA1 at day 1 but recovered to baseline level by day 7; the other population did not change at day 1 but showed significant up-regulations of sGluA1 at day 7.
source: We observed two populations of dendrites: one population showed decrease of sGluA1 at day 1 but recovered to baseline level by day 7; The other population of dendrites did not change at day 1 but showed significant up-regulations of sGluA1 at day 7 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D comparing dendrites that decreased vs. did not decrease at day 1.

claim: About 51% of dendrites showed decrease at day 1 following visual deprivation.
source: The percentage of decrease dendrites was about 51% (Figure 4E, for details, see Methods).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The two distinct populations of dendrites did not result from different populations of neurons, as dendrites from the same neuron still responded differentially to deprivation.
source: These two distinct populations of dendrites did not result from different populations of neurons, as we found that dendrites from the same neuron still responded differentially to deprivation (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4F showing different responses from dendrites of the same neuron.

claim: There are two populations of spines with distinct responses to enucleation.
source: Similarly, we observed two populations of spines with distinct responses to the enucleation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 2 days of visual deprivation is sufficient to increase AMPAR-mediated mEPSC amplitude in V1 L2/3 neurons in ex vivo studies.
source: Previous studies using electrophysiological recordings in acute brain slices have reported that 2 days of visual deprivation is sufficient to increase AMPAR-mediated mEPSC amplitude in V1 L2/3 neurons (Bridi et al., 2018; Goel and Lee, 2007), however, we didn't observe any changes in synaptic AMPAR expression at that time point in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Bridi et al. and Goel and Lee.

claim: Synaptic GluA1 but not GluN1 was significantly increased in V1 synaptosomes from mice 2 days after binocular enucleation.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Bridi et al., 2018; Goel and Lee, 2007), we observed a significant increase in synaptic GluA1 but not GluN1 in enucleated mice (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Synaptic GluA1 in L1 was decreased 2 days after enucleation but subsequently recovered to baseline by day 7.
source: The experiment revealed that synaptic GluA1 in L1 was decreased 2 days after enucleation but subsequently recovered to baseline by day 7, whereas synaptic GluA1 expression in L2-6 significantly increased following 2 days of enucleation and remained enhanced at day 7 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data from layer-specific dissections shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Synaptic GluA1 expression in L2-6 significantly increased following 2 days of enucleation and remained enhanced at day 7.
source: The experiment revealed that synaptic GluA1 in L1 was decreased 2 days after enucleation but subsequently recovered to baseline by day 7, whereas synaptic GluA1 expression in L2-6 significantly increased following 2 days of enucleation and remained enhanced at day 7 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data from layer-specific dissections shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Visual deprivation has distinct effects on AMPAR expression in spines located in different layers.
source: These data suggest that visual deprivation has distinct effects on AMPAR expression in spines located in different layers.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that L1 and L2-6 show different temporal patterns of GluA1 changes.

claim: The amount of spine sGluA1 on basal dendrites was significantly increased 1 day following enucleation and remained elevated afterwards.
source: To verify this in vivo, we repeatedly imaged basal dendrites from L2/3 neurons (150–300 μm deep) before and after enucleation. The amount of spine sGluA1 on basal dendrites was significantly increased 1 day following enucleation and remained elevated afterwards (Figure 5E,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Spine sGluA1 increases were consistently and significantly larger on basal dendrites than on apical dendrites of the same neurons following visual deprivation.
source: To confirm that the difference in time course between basal dendrites and apical dendrites in response to deprivation is dependent on locations rather than resulting from different populations of neurons being examined, we imaged both apical dendrites and basal dendrites from the same neurons. We found that spine sGluA1 increases were consistently and significantly larger on basal dendrites than on apical dendrites (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by imaging data from the same neurons shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The ratios of relative change in spine sGluA1 from basal dendrites over apical dendrites were significantly larger than one following deprivation.
source: The ratios of relative change in spine sGluA1 from basal dendrites over apical dendrites were significantly larger than one following deprivation (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Spines on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons increase GluA1 content faster and more robustly than spines on apical dendrites in response to visual deprivation.
source: Taken together, these data reveal that spines on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons increase GluA1 content faster and more robustly than spines on apical dendrites in response to visual deprivation.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that basal dendrites show earlier and larger increases than apical dendrites.

claim: The change of average spine sGluA1 expression level on dendrites after 7 days of enucleation was positively correlated with the depth of dendrites.
source: The change of average spine sGluA1 expression level on dendrites after 7 days of enucleation was positively correlated with the depth of dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E), indicating that deep dendrites have greater increases than superficial dendrites.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Deep dendrites have greater increases in sGluA1 than superficial dendrites following visual deprivation.
source: The change of average spine sGluA1 expression level on dendrites after 7 days of enucleation was positively correlated with the depth of dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E), indicating that deep dendrites have greater increases than superficial dendrites.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between depth and sGluA1 change.

claim: In both ascending dendrites and descending dendrites, there was a positive correlation between spine depth and deprivation-induced sGluA1 expression.
source: In both ascending dendrites and descending dendrites, there was a positive correlation between spine depth and deprivation-induced sGluA1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), such that deep spines increase sGluA1 more than superficial spines following deprivation.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Deep spines increase sGluA1 more than superficial spines following deprivation.
source: In both ascending dendrites and descending dendrites, there was a positive correlation between spine depth and deprivation-induced sGluA1 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), such that deep spines increase sGluA1 more than superficial spines following deprivation.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between spine depth and sGluA1 change.

claim: The correlation of spine sGluA1 change with the distance from dendrite branch point showed opposite directions in ascending and descending dendrites.
source: Significantly, the correlation of spine sGluA1 change with the distance from dendrite branch point showed opposite directions in ascending and descending dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that changes in sGluA1 expression are correlated with spine depth instead of distance from dendrite branch point.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Changes in sGluA1 expression are correlated with spine depth instead of distance from dendrite branch point.
source: Significantly, the correlation of spine sGluA1 change with the distance from dendrite branch point showed opposite directions in ascending and descending dendrites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that changes in sGluA1 expression are correlated with spine depth instead of distance from dendrite branch point.
evidence: Inferred from the opposite correlations with distance in ascending vs. descending dendrites but consistent positive correlation with depth.

claim: Baseline expression of spine sGluA1 was positively correlated with the distance from branch point but not with the depth of spines.
source: Second, when we focused on baseline expression of spine sGluA1, we found it was positively correlated with the distance from branch point but not with the depth of spines (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: In both apical and basal dendrites, spines positioned more deeply from the pia exhibited greater deprivation-induced changes in synaptic sGluA1 expression than spines more superficially poised along the same dendrite.
source: In both apical and basal dendrites we found that spines positioned more deeply from the pia exhibited greater deprivation-induced changes in synaptic sGluA1 expression than spines more superficially poised along the same dendrite (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K comparing deep vs. superficial spines.

claim: Visual deprivation induces depth-dependent changes in spine sGluA1.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that visual deprivation induces depth-dependent changes in spine sGluA1.
evidence: Inferred from multiple analyses showing correlation between depth and sGluA1 changes.

claim: L4 scaling occurs only before P21 in visual cortex.
source: Laminar differences have been reported for ex vivo measurements of homeostatic synaptic scaling induced by visual deprivation, where L4 scaling occurs only before P21, and L2/3 scaling is observed only after this age (Desai et al., 2002; Petrus et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Desai et al. and Petrus et al.

claim: L2/3 scaling is observed only after P21 in visual cortex.
source: Laminar differences have been reported for ex vivo measurements of homeostatic synaptic scaling induced by visual deprivation, where L4 scaling occurs only before P21, and L2/3 scaling is observed only after this age (Desai et al., 2002; Petrus et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Desai et al. and Petrus et al.

claim: 7 days of enucleation did not induce a change of synaptic GluA1 expression in L1 in biochemical experiments.
source: Additionally, 7 days of enucleation did not induce a change of synaptic GluA1 expression in L1 in our in vitro biochemical experiments but caused a significant increase in spine sGluA1 level on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons in vivo.
evidence: Supported by biochemical data from layer-specific dissections.

claim: 7 days of enucleation caused a significant increase in spine sGluA1 level on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons in vivo.
source: Additionally, 7 days of enucleation did not induce a change of synaptic GluA1 expression in L1 in our in vitro biochemical experiments but caused a significant increase in spine sGluA1 level on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data.

claim: Under baseline conditions, average spine sGluA1 expression on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was very stable.
source: Under baseline conditions we found that average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size on apical dendrites of L5 neurons were very stable with 66% spines persisting across 10 imaging days (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Under baseline conditions, spine size on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was very stable.
source: Under baseline conditions we found that average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size on apical dendrites of L5 neurons were very stable with 66% spines persisting across 10 imaging days (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 66% of spines on apical dendrites of L5 neurons persisted across 10 imaging days under baseline conditions.
source: Under baseline conditions we found that average spine sGluA1 expression and spine size on apical dendrites of L5 neurons were very stable with 66% spines persisting across 10 imaging days (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: sGluA1 intensity within individual spines on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was very dynamic.
source: Similar to L2/3 neurons, sGluA1 intensity within individual spines on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was very dynamic as well.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of dynamic changes in individual spine sGluA1 levels over time.

claim: The average CV of spine sGluA1 signal on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was significantly smaller than that on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons.
source: However, the average CV of spine sGluA1 signal on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was significantly smaller than that on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons (Figure 6C), indicating that L5 neurons are less dynamic than L2/3 neurons.
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: L5 neurons are less dynamic than L2/3 neurons.
source: However, the average CV of spine sGluA1 signal on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was significantly smaller than that on apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons (Figure 6C), indicating that L5 neurons are less dynamic than L2/3 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the smaller CV in L5 neurons compared to L2/3 neurons.

claim: L2/3 neurons receive more feedforward inputs from L4 than L5 neurons.
source: Since L2/3 neurons receive more feedforward inputs from L4 than L5 neurons, the higher dynamic observed in L2/3 neurons suggests that sensory input is a drive for synaptic AMPAR dynamic.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cortical circuit organization.

claim: The higher dynamic observed in L2/3 neurons suggests that sensory input is a drive for synaptic AMPAR dynamic.
source: Since L2/3 neurons receive more feedforward inputs from L4 than L5 neurons, the higher dynamic observed in L2/3 neurons suggests that sensory input is a drive for synaptic AMPAR dynamic.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between input patterns and dynamics.

claim: The spine survival rate of L5 neurons remained unchanged following visual deprivation.
source: Following visual deprivation, the spine survival rate of L5 neurons remained unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but the CV of spine sGluA1 level was increased (Figure 6D), further suggesting that this dynamic is dependent on sensory input.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The CV of spine sGluA1 level in L5 neurons was increased following visual deprivation.
source: Following visual deprivation, the spine survival rate of L5 neurons remained unchanged (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), but the CV of spine sGluA1 level was increased (Figure 6D), further suggesting that this dynamic is dependent on sensory input.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Spine sGluA1 expression on apical dendrites of L5 neurons was reduced after 1 day of visual deprivation and then recovered to baseline levels.
source: Regarding synaptic AMPAR expression, we observed that spine sGluA1 expression was reduced after 1 day and then recovered to baseline levels (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: No significant increase in spine sGluA1 was observed after 7 days of deprivation in L5 neurons.
source: Nevertheless, in contrast to L2/3 neurons, we didn't observe any significant increase after 7 days of deprivation in L5 neurons (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Visual deprivation specifically enhances AMPAR expression on apical dendrites of V1 L2/3 neurons but not on apical dendrites of L5 neurons.
source: We therefore conclude that visual deprivation specifically enhances AMPAR expression on apical dendrites of V1 L2/3 neurons but not on apical dendrites of L5 neurons, intriguingly suggesting exclusive mechanisms that regulate these distinct cortical circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the differential responses between L2/3 and L5 neurons.

claim: There are two populations of L5 cells with distinct responses to visual deprivation: one group showed decrease at day 1 and day 2 after enucleation and then recovered to baseline later while the other group did not decrease at day 1 but exhibited a gradual increase following enucleation.
source: We then categorized cells based on whether their apical dendrites did or did not display a decrease after 1 day of enucleation, and we found that there were two populations of cells with distinct responses to binocular deprivations: one group showed decrease at day 1 and day 2 after enucleation and then recovered to baseline later while the other group did not decrease at day 1 but exhibited a gradual increase following enucleation despite that increases were not significant at any time points compared to the baseline level (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The two populations of L5 cells with distinct responses to visual deprivation might be due to their different cell types.
source: Previous studies in the barrel cortex indicate that specific subtypes of L5 neurons respond differentially to changes in sensory experiences (Greenhill et al., 2015; Holtmaat et al., 2006). The two populations of cells in V1 L5 with distinct responses to visual deprivation observed here might be due to their different cell types.
evidence: Speculated based on previous findings in barrel cortex and the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The change of synaptic sGluA1 expression on dendrites in L5 neurons did not correlate with the depth.
source: The change of synaptic sGluA1 expression on dendrites did not correlate with the depth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In L5 neurons, there were no correlations between the change in spine sGluA1 and spine depth in both sham-surgery and VD groups.
source: For individual spines, in both sham-surgery and VD groups, we did not see any correlations between the change in spine sGluA1 and spine depth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between baseline spine sGluA1 level and the distance to dendrite branch point in L5 neurons.
source: Nevertheless, there was a strong positive correlation between baseline spine sGluA1 level and the distance to dendrite branch point in L5 neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The depth-dependent changes of spine sGluA1 induced by deprivation are specific to L2/3 neurons.
source: These results indicate that the depth-dependent changes of spine sGluA1 induced by deprivation are specific to L2/3 neurons as well.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that depth-dependent changes occur in L2/3 but not L5 neurons.

claim: The distance-dependent baseline expression of spine sGluA1 occurs in both L2/3 and L5 neurons.
source: However, the distance-dependent baseline expression of spine sGluA1 occurs in both L2/3 and L5 neurons, suggesting that this is a more general phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both cell types show correlation between baseline sGluA1 and distance from branch point.

claim: GRIP1 plays a key role in regulating AMPAR trafficking, synaptic targeting and homeostatic plasticity.
source: We have previously shown that GRIP1 plays a key role in regulating AMPAR trafficking, synaptic targeting and homeostatic plasticity (Gainey et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2010; Pfennig et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: In wild type mice, there was a significant increase in synaptic GluA1 as well as GRIP1 in V1 after 2 days of enucleation.
source: In wild type (WT) mice, using biochemical experiments we identified a significant increase in synaptic GluA1 as well as GRIP1 in V1 after 2 days of enucleation as described above (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: No increase in synaptic GluA1 was observed in Grip1 knockout mice following visual deprivation.
source: However, no increase in synaptic GluA1 was observed in Grip1 knockout mice (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: Supported by biochemical data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: No increases of spine sGluA1 on apical dendrites of V1 L2/3 neurons were observed in Grip1 knockout mice in vivo following enucleation.
source: Moreover, we observed no increases of spine sGluA1 on apical dendrites of V1 L2/3 neurons in Grip1 knockout mice in vivo following enucleation.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from Grip1 knockout mice.

claim: A small decrease in spine sGluA1 level was observed in Grip1 knockout mice that recovered between day 3 and day 7 after deprivation.
source: In fact, we observed a small decrease in spine sGluA1 level that recovered between day 3 and day 7 after deprivation (Figure 7D,E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The initial decrease of sGluA1 after enucleation in Grip1 knockout mice phenocopies results from WT mice.
source: The initial decrease of sGluA1 after enucleation phenocopies our results from WT mice (Figure 3B) and might be extended in Grip1 knockout mice due to reduced AMPAR exocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with WT results and known function of GRIP1.

claim: The later recovery of sGluA1 in Grip1 knockout mice could be some compensatory regulations by other AMPAR-binding proteins, like GRIP2.
source: The later recovery could be some compensatory regulations by other AMPAR-binding proteins, like GRIP2 (Anggono and Huganir, 2012).
evidence: Speculated based on known compensatory mechanisms and cited literature.

claim: GRIP1 is essential for the deprivation-induced up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs.
source: Nevertheless, these data demonstrate that GRIP1 is essential for the deprivation-induced up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of up-regulation in Grip1 knockout mice.

claim: Synaptic expression of AMPARs is highly dynamic in mice with normal experience despite the relatively stable overall expression.
source: AMPAR trafficking is critical for synaptic plasticity and brain function (Anggono and Huganir, 2012; Huganir and Nicoll, 2013; Volk et al., 2015). We show that synaptic expression of AMPARs is highly dynamic in mice with normal experience despite the relatively stable overall expression, suggesting that strength of individual synapses is continuously being modified.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing dynamic changes in individual spines despite stable averages.

claim: Strength of individual synapses is continuously being modified.
source: We show that synaptic expression of AMPARs is highly dynamic in mice with normal experience despite the relatively stable overall expression, suggesting that strength of individual synapses is continuously being modified.
evidence: Inferred from the dynamic changes in individual spine sGluA1 levels.

claim: Sensory input is a drive for synaptic AMPAR dynamic.
source: Since L2/3 neurons receive more feedforward inputs from L4 than L5 neurons, the higher dynamic observed in L2/3 neurons suggests that sensory input is a drive for synaptic AMPAR dynamic. Moreover, depriving the visual input greatly changes the dynamics of V1, shifting from L2/3 to L5, which further supports that this dynamic is driven by sensory inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between input patterns, dynamics, and effects of deprivation.

claim: Depriving the visual input greatly changes the dynamics of V1, shifting from L2/3 to L5.
source: Moreover, depriving the visual input greatly changes the dynamics of V1, shifting from L2/3 to L5, which further supports that this dynamic is driven by sensory inputs.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased CV in L5 and decreased CV in L2/3 after deprivation.

claim: Synaptic strength and spine size are well correlated.
source: Synaptic strength and spine size are well correlated, and synaptic potentiation or depression is usually accompanied with an increase or decrease in spine size, respectively (Bosch et al., 2014; Makino and Malinow, 2009).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations to previous studies.

claim: Synaptic potentiation or depression is usually accompanied with an increase or decrease in spine size, respectively.
source: Synaptic strength and spine size are well correlated, and synaptic potentiation or depression is usually accompanied with an increase or decrease in spine size, respectively (Bosch et al., 2014; Makino and Malinow, 2009).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations to previous studies.

claim: Synaptic sGluA1 shows greater changes than spine size following visual deprivation.
source: Nevertheless, we do find a small population of spines that exhibit a divergence of spine form and function. Moreover, synaptic sGluA1 shows greater changes than spine size following visual deprivation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of sGluA1 and spine size changes in the data.

claim: Differences in synaptic strength may be underestimated or even not correctly determined when using spine size as a measurement.
source: These suggest that differences in synaptic strength may be underestimated or even not correctly determined when using spine size as a measurement.
evidence: Inferred from observations of divergence between spine size and sGluA1 changes.

claim: The dissociation of spine size and synaptic strength has been reported many times.
source: Indeed, the dissociation of spine size and synaptic strength has been reported many times (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Spine number or volume is not changed at all at cerebellar Purkinje cell synapses during LTD.
source: Spine number or volume is not changed at all at cerebellar Purkinje cell synapses during LTD (Sdrulla and Linden, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Insulin-induced endocytosis of AMPARs is not accompanied by spine shrinkage.
source: Insulin-induced endocytosis of AMPARs is not accompanied by spine shrinkage (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Spine size and AMPAR function are coupled through some common signaling mechanisms, but there is a divergence in the downstream signaling pathways that regulate these two processes.
source: Spine size and AMPAR function are coupled through some common signaling mechanisms, but there is a divergence in the downstream signaling pathways that regulate these two processes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of synaptic signaling mechanisms.

claim: Spine shrinkage is mediated by cofilin while LTD is dependent on protein phosphatase one although both require calcium influx through NMDA receptors and enhanced calcineurin activity.
source: For instance, it has been shown that spine shrinkage is mediated by cofilin while LTD is dependent on protein phosphatase one although both require calcium influx through NMDA receptors and enhanced calcineurin activity (Zhou et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Spine size, in certain conditions, is not a good indication of synaptic strength.
source: Thus, spine size, in certain conditions, is not a good indication of synaptic strength, and our imaging of synaptic AMPAR expression provides a direct and accurate way to monitor functional changes at synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of dissociation between spine size and AMPAR expression.

claim: Imaging of synaptic AMPAR expression provides a direct and accurate way to monitor functional changes at synapses.
source: Thus, spine size, in certain conditions, is not a good indication of synaptic strength, and our imaging of synaptic AMPAR expression provides a direct and accurate way to monitor functional changes at synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between SEP-GluA1 intensity and uEPSC amplitude.

claim: Synapses express a varying number of AMPARs that increases with distance from the soma, a phenomenon known as distance-dependent scaling.
source: To overcome the filtering and attenuation caused by the cable properties of dendrites (Rall, 1962a; Rall, 1962b), synapses express a varying number of AMPARs that increases with distance from the soma, a phenomenon known as distance-dependent scaling (Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both L2/3 and L5 cortical pyramidal neurons display a distance-dependent baseline expression of sGluA1, wherein distal spines have higher levels of sGluA1 than proximal spines.
source: Here, we find that both L2/3 and L5 cortical pyramidal neurons display a distance-dependent baseline expression of sGluA1, wherein distal spines have higher levels of sGluA1 than proximal spines.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing positive correlation between baseline sGluA1 and distance from branch point.

claim: The distance-dependent scaling of AMPARs might be a general phenomenon across brain regions.
source: These results suggest that the distance-dependent scaling of AMPARs might be a general phenomenon across brain regions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both hippocampal and cortical neurons show this phenomenon.

claim: Chronic visual deprivation leads to synaptic enrichment of AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons through synaptic scaling mechanisms in ex vivo studies.
source: Many studies using ex vivo acute slices have shown that chronic visual deprivation leads to synaptic enrichment of AMPARs in V1 L2/3 neurons through synaptic scaling mechanisms (Goel and Lee, 2007; He et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in spine sGluA1 expression induced by visual deprivation are highly heterogeneous in live animals.
source: Using in vivo imaging of fluorescently labeled AMPARs, we were able to track individual spine changes before and after visual deprivation, thus providing unprecedented levels of spatiotemporal information regarding synaptic AMPAR dynamics. We determined that changes in spine sGluA1 expression induced by visual deprivation are highly heterogeneous in live animals and only a subset of spines undergoes potentiation.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing heterogeneous responses of individual spines.

claim: Potentiated synapses following visual deprivation are spatially organized and tend to be located deep within L2/3 neurons, predominately on basal rather than apical dendrites.
source: These potentiated synapses are spatially organized and tend to be located deep within L2/3 neurons, predominately on basal rather than apical dendrites, and this depth-dependent mechanism even applies to spines along the same dendrite, indicating that deprivation-induced changes are compartment- and input-specific, as apical dendrites and basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons receive different inputs (Ko et al., 2011; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Petrus et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing depth-dependent and compartment-specific changes.

claim: Deprivation-induced changes are compartment- and input-specific, as apical dendrites and basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons receive different inputs.
source: These potentiated synapses are spatially organized and tend to be located deep within L2/3 neurons, predominately on basal rather than apical dendrites, and this depth-dependent mechanism even applies to spines along the same dendrite, indicating that deprivation-induced changes are compartment- and input-specific, as apical dendrites and basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons receive different inputs (Ko et al., 2011; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Petrus et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the differential responses between compartments and supported by citations about input patterns.

claim: The expression pattern of neurotransmitter receptors varies in different layers.
source: In addition, it has been shown that the expression pattern of neurotransmitter receptors varies in different layers, and thus other extracellular factors like neuromodulators could also contribute to this depth-dependent plasticity (Brombas et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Extracellular factors like neuromodulators could contribute to depth-dependent plasticity.
source: In addition, it has been shown that the expression pattern of neurotransmitter receptors varies in different layers, and thus other extracellular factors like neuromodulators could also contribute to this depth-dependent plasticity (Brombas et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculated based on known layer-specific expression patterns and cited literature.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity is generally thought to occur globally throughout the neuron, but it can also occur locally.
source: Although homeostatic plasticity is generally thought to occur globally throughout the neuron, it can also occur locally (Béïque et al., 2011; Turrigiano, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The visual deprivation-induced homeostatic up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs is synapse-specific.
source: Our results reveal that the visual deprivation-induced homeostatic up-regulation of synaptic AMPARs is synapse-specific.
evidence: Inferred from the heterogeneous and spatially organized responses of individual synapses.

claim: The increase observed after 2 days ex vivo is primarily caused by the increase of synaptic sGluA1 on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons.
source: The increase in spine sGluA1 on the apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons occurred after 7 days of visual deprivation while in V1 region from the acute brain slice we saw a significant elevation of synaptic GluA1 after 2 days of deprivation. That discrepancy led us to investigate the changes happening on the basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons. Indeed, we observed that the amount of synaptic sGluA1 on the basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons was significantly increased after one day of deprivation and remained elevated afterwards. Therefore, the increase observed after 2 days ex vivo is primarily caused by the increase of synaptic sGluA1 on basal dendrites of L2/3 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that basal dendrites show early increases while apical dendrites do not.

claim: Synaptic sGluA1 on the apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons decreases first following visual deprivation.
source: As far as we know, our study is the first report to show that synaptic sGluA1 on the apical dendrites of L2/3 neurons decreases first following visual deprivation.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing initial decrease at day 1.

claim: The dendrites that show the initial decrease following visual deprivation are located in the superficial region and they probably receive top-down inputs from regions like retrosplenial cortex and cingulate.
source: The dendrites that show the initial decrease are located in the superficial region and they probably receive top-down inputs from regions like retrosplenial cortex and cingulate (Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Roth et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the location of dendrites and supported by citations about input patterns.

claim: Visual deprivation may induce LTD that results in reduced synaptic AMPAR level in connections receiving top-down inputs.
source: Visual deprivation may induce LTD that results in reduced synaptic AMPAR level in those connections.
evidence: Speculated based on the observed decrease in superficial dendrites.

claim: Visual-deprivation-induced homeostatic plasticity is lamina-specific and age-dependent in V1.
source: Visual-deprivation-induced homeostatic plasticity has been reported to be lamina-specific and age-dependent in V1.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in the following sentences.

claim: In L6, dark exposure initiated before but not after P21 increases average amplitude of mEPSC.
source: In L6, dark exposure initiated before but not after P21 increases average amplitude of mEPSC (Petrus et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Visual deprivation induces an increase in spine size and mEPSC amplitude of L5 neurons in adult mice.
source: Regarding L5 neurons, visual deprivation induces an increase in spine size and mEPSC amplitude of L5 neurons in adult mice (Barnes et al., 2017; Keck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A complete loss of visually driven cortical activity is required to elicit homeostatic plasticity in V1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Notably, a study has carefully and systematically investigated how varying visual deprivation paradigms affect plasticity in V1 and demonstrates that a complete loss of visually driven cortical activity is required to elicit homeostatic plasticity in V1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (He et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Binocular enucleation successfully induces up-regulation of synaptic sGluA1 in V1 L2/3 neurons.
source: Here, we used binocular enucleation to completely deprive visual inputs and showed that this paradigm successfully induces up-regulation of synaptic sGluA1 in V1 L2/3 neurons, which is consistent with previous ex vivo studies.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing increases in sGluA1 after enucleation.

claim: The increase in mEPSC amplitude of L5 neurons induced by visual deprivation could be contributed by the basal dendrites.
source: The increase in mEPSC amplitude of L5 neurons induced by visual deprivation could be contributed by the basal dendrites, as here we only imaged the apical dendrites of L5 neurons.
evidence: Speculated based on the limitation that only apical dendrites were imaged.

claim: In the barrel cortex there is distinct plasticity triggered by sensory changes in specific subtypes of L5 neurons.
source: In addition, it has been shown that in the barrel cortex there is distinct plasticity triggered by sensory changes in specific subtypes of L5 neurons (Greenhill et al., 2015; Holtmaat et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of a sensory input leads to widespread changes across brain areas, including the deprived sensory cortex and spared sensory cortices.
source: Emerging evidence has shown that loss of a sensory input leads to widespread changes across brain areas, including the deprived sensory cortex and spared sensory cortices (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Lee and Whitt, 2015; Petrus et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visual deprivation produces compensatory changes in other spared sensory cortices, such as somatosensory cortex and auditory cortex, with decreases of mEPSC amplitude in L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: For example, visual deprivation not only induces homeostatic plasticity in primary visual cortex, but also produces compensatory changes in other spared sensory cortices, such as somatosensory cortex and auditory cortex, with decreases of mEPSC amplitude in L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Lee and Whitt, 2015; Petrus et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of vision caused a reduction in synaptic sGluA1 of L2/3 neurons within non-V1 visual cortex.
source: In the study, we showed that loss of vision caused a reduction in synaptic sGluA1 of L2/3 neurons within non-V1 visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from non-V1 visual cortex.

claim: Non-V1 visual cortex exhibited a much earlier decrease in sGluA1 compared to somatosensory and auditory cortices.
source: Notably, unlike somatosensory and auditory cortices, non-V1 visual cortex exhibited a much earlier decrease.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of timing of changes between non-V1 visual cortex and other spared sensory cortices.

claim: The adaptation of brain circuits within visual cortex is different from those in spared sensory cortices.
source: Therefore, the adaptation of brain circuits within visual cortex is different from those in spared sensory cortices.
evidence: Inferred from the different patterns of changes observed in visual cortex vs. other sensory cortices.

claim: The adult brain remains remarkably malleable and is continuously reshaped by experience.
source: Our study supports the notion that the adult brain remains remarkably malleable and is continuously reshaped by experience.
evidence: Inferred from the observations of dynamic changes and plasticity in adult animals.
